claim: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast.
source: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast, which has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established scientific literature and consensus in the field.

claim: Speed underestimation at low contrast has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
source: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast, which has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence: This claim references a hypothesis from prior research literature.

claim: Speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene independently of their distance from the viewer.
source: we confirm that speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene independently of their distance from the viewer.
evidence: This claim is confirmed by experimental data from the study's psychophysics measurements and driving simulation.

claim: When contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated.
source: However, we show that when contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated, prompting drivers to decelerate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Speed overestimation in fog prompts drivers to decelerate.
source: However, we show that when contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated, prompting drivers to decelerate.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the driving simulation experiments.

claim: Perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene rather than the global level of contrast per se.
source: we demonstrate for the first time that perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene rather than the global level of contrast per se.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated through experimental data comparing fog and anti-fog conditions with identical global contrast.

claim: Visual contrast is usually referred to as the difference in brightness between an object and the background.
source: Visual contrast is usually referred to as the difference in brightness between an object and the background (Hofstetter et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Classical vision research experiments systematically investigated how visual contrast affects objects motion perception.
source: Classical vision research experiments systematically investigated how visual contrast affects objects motion perception (Thompson, 1982; Stone and Thompson, 1992; Blakemore and Snowden, 1999; Anstis, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The perceived speed of two-dimensional moving objects is underestimated when visual contrast is reduced.
source: These studies have shown that the perceived speed of two-dimensional moving objects—for example, plaid patterns on a computer screen—is underestimated when visual contrast is reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research studies.

claim: The underestimation of visual speed at low contrast applies also to perceived self-motion in three-dimensional environments.
source: More recent studies based on driving scenarios have suggested that the underestimation of visual speed at low contrast applies also to perceived self-motion in three-dimensional environments (Snowden et al., 1998; Horswill and Plooy, 2008; Owens et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent driving scenario studies.

claim: Speed underestimation at low contrast was proposed as a possible explanation for excessive driving speed in fog.
source: This finding was proposed—and is still considered—as a possible explanation for excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence: This claim references a hypothesis from prior research.

claim: In all studies having assessed the effect of visual contrast on motion perception, contrast was reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene, irrespective of their distance from the observer.
source: In the abovementioned studies, and more generally in all studies having assessed the effect of visual contrast on motion perception, contrast was reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene, irrespective of their distance from the observer.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of prior research literature.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen.
source: While uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen, it is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the appropriateness of experimental methods.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
source: While uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen, it is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the limitations of experimental methods.

claim: Fog alters visual contrast because tiny water droplets suspended in the air are interposed between the observer and the surrounding objects.
source: Specifically, fog alters visual contrast because tiny water droplets suspended in the air are interposed between the observer and the surrounding objects.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the physical properties of fog.

claim: The quantity of droplets increases along the line-of-sight as distance from the observer increases in fog.
source: The quantity of droplets increases along the line-of-sight as distance from the observer increases.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about fog physics.

claim: The contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance in fog.
source: As a consequence, the contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance, and visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the physical properties of fog.

claim: In fog, visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
source: As a consequence, the contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance, and visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the physical properties of fog.

claim: The distance-dependent attenuation of contrast experienced in fog is very different from the uniform reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
source: Therefore, the distance-dependent attenuation of contrast experienced in fog is obviously very different from the uniform reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference comparing two types of contrast reduction.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction resembles more closely what one could experience when looking at the environment through a dirty glass or a foggy windshield.
source: Uniform contrast reduction resembles more closely what one could experience when looking at the environment through a dirty glass or a foggy windshield.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about real-world scenarios.

claim: The effects of distance-dependent contrast reduction on motion perception are unknown.
source: To date, the effects of distance-dependent contrast reduction on motion perception are unknown.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature showing a gap in knowledge.

claim: We still do not know how fog affects perceived self-motion.
source: In other words, we still do not know how fog affects perceived self-motion.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature showing a gap in knowledge.

claim: Twelve experienced drivers were presented with pairs of driving scenes and instructed to estimate which scene moved faster in the first experiment.
source: Twelve experienced drivers were presented with pairs of driving scenes and instructed to estimate which scene moved faster (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology and is supported by the experimental design.

claim: One of the scenes (reference) had clear visibility and moved at one of three target speeds (40, 60, or 90 km/hr).
source: One of the scenes (reference) had clear visibility and moved at one of three target speeds (40, 60, or 90 km/hr).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The test scene had either clear or reduced visibility, and its speed was adjusted for each trial using a Bayesian adaptive method.
source: The other scene (test) had either clear or reduced visibility, and its speed was adjusted for each trial using a Bayesian adaptive method (Kontsevich and Tyler, 1999).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology with citation to the method.

claim: The Bayesian adaptive method allowed determination of the point of subjective equality (PSE) and the just-noticeable difference (JND).
source: This method allowed us to determine the point of subjective equality (PSE) as well as the just-noticeable difference (JND).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology and measurements.

claim: The PSE corresponded to the speed at which the two scenes were perceived as moving equally fast.
source: The PSE corresponded to the speed at which the two scenes were perceived as moving equally fast.
evidence: This claim defines a measurement used in the study.

claim: PSEs higher than the actual speed of the reference scene indicated speed underestimation.
source: Therefore, PSEs higher than the actual speed of the reference scene indicated speed underestimation, whereas PSEs lower than the speed of the reference scene indicated speed overestimation.

claim: PSEs lower than the speed of the reference scene indicated speed overestimation.
source: Therefore, PSEs higher than the actual speed of the reference scene indicated speed underestimation, whereas PSEs lower than the speed of the reference scene indicated speed overestimation.
evidence: This claim defines the interpretation of measurements.

claim: The JND corresponded to the smallest detectable difference between two different speeds.
source: The JND corresponded to the smallest detectable difference between two different speeds.
evidence: This claim defines a measurement used in the study.

claim: High JNDs indicated low discrimination sensitivity.
source: High JNDs indicated low discrimination sensitivity, whereas low JNDs indicated high discrimination sensitivity.
evidence: This claim defines the interpretation of measurements.

claim: Low JNDs indicated high discrimination sensitivity.
source: High JNDs indicated low discrimination sensitivity, whereas low JNDs indicated high discrimination sensitivity.
evidence: This claim defines the interpretation of measurements.

claim: The contrast of the scene was reduced either in a distance-dependent manner, as would happen in natural fog, or in a distance-independent manner, as has been done in previous experiments.
source: The contrast of the scene was reduced either in a distance-dependent manner, as would happen in natural fog, or in a distance-independent manner, as has been done in previous experiments.

claim: The difference between distance-dependent and distance-independent contrast reduction is represented in Figure 2B and C.
source: The difference between these two types of contrast reduction is represented in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Moderate and severe levels of reduction were implemented for each type of contrast alteration.
source: Moderate and severe levels of reduction were implemented for each type of contrast alteration.

claim: For each level of reduction, the overall visual contrast was the same for distance-dependent and distance-independent alteration.
source: Importantly, for each level of reduction, the overall visual contrast was the same for distance-dependent and distance-independent alteration (Root mean square [RMS] contrast = 0.31 for moderate visibility reduction and 0.19 for severe visibility reduction, vs 0.46 for clear visibility).

claim: RMS contrast was 0.31 for moderate visibility reduction.

claim: RMS contrast was 0.19 for severe visibility reduction.

source: In total, the experiment consisted of five visibility conditions: clear (no contrast reduction), moderate and severe fog (distance-dependent contrast reduction), moderate and severe uniform reduction (distance-independent contrast reduction).

claim: Reducing the contrast of the visual scene altered speed perception (F(4,44) = 52.086, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.61).
source: Reducing the contrast of the visual scene altered speed perception [F(4,44) = 52.086, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.61].

claim: Perceived speed was affected differently by the two types of contrast reduction.

claim: When contrast reduction depended on distance, participants matched lower speeds (PSE mean = 54.7 and 41.7 km/hr for moderate and severe fog, respectively) to the perceived speed under clear visibility (mean = 65 km/hr).
source: Specifically, when contrast reduction depended on distance, participants matched lower speeds (PSE mean = 54.7 and 41.7 km/hr for moderate and severe fog, respectively) to the perceived speed under clear visibility (mean = 65 km/hr).

claim: Natural fog led to an overestimation of speed (equivalent to 76.4 and 94.3 km/hr for moderate and severe fog, respectively).

claim: Speed was underestimated with uniform contrast reduction (perceived speed equivalent to 41.4 and 41.5 km/hr for moderate and severe reduction, respectively).
source: Therefore, speed was underestimated with uniform contrast reduction (perceived speed equivalent to 41.4 and 41.5 km/hr for moderate and severe reduction, respectively).
evidence: This claim is based on calculated values from experimental data.

claim: Each condition differed from each of the others (p<0.05), except for uniform-moderate and uniform-severe reduction that did not differ significantly from one another.

claim: The same pattern of results was observed for all three target speeds.
source: The same pattern of results was observed for all three target speeds.

claim: The two types of contrast reduction gave rise to opposite perceptual effects.

claim: The participants had more difficulties estimating the driving speed when visibility reduction was independent of distance.
source: This indicates that the participants had more difficulties estimating the driving speed when visibility reduction was independent of distance.

claim: The reduction of speed discrimination sensitivity might result from the fact that distance-independent contrast alteration is seldom encountered in real life.
source: This reduction of speed discrimination sensitivity might result from the fact that distance-independent contrast alteration is seldom encountered in real life.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the cause of observed effects.

claim: Drivers usually demist their windshield before starting to drive.
source: Specifically, although entering a car with a foggy windshield is common, especially due to cold weather, drivers usually demist their windshield before starting to drive.
evidence: This claim is based on common knowledge about driving behavior.

claim: Drivers' options to reduce environmental fog are much more restricted.
source: Unfortunately, drivers' options to reduce environmental fog are much more restricted.

claim: Ten experienced drivers who did not participate in the first experiment were instructed to drive at target speeds with either clear or reduced visibility in the second experiment.
source: In the second experiment, we tested whether the perceptual changes measured in the first experiment affect actual driving behaviour. Ten experienced drivers who did not participate in the first experiment were instructed to drive at target speeds with either clear or reduced visibility.

claim: The visibility conditions and target speeds in experiment 2 were the same as in experiment 1.
source: The visibility conditions and target speeds were the same as in experiment 1.

claim: In the training phase, drivers learned to reach and maintain each target speed with clear visibility.
source: In a preliminary training phase, drivers learned to reach and maintain each target speed with clear visibility (Figure 1B, left pane).

claim: In the test phase, drivers freely controlled their driving speed with the gas pedal, and pressed a button when thinking they were driving at target speed.
source: In the test phase, drivers freely controlled their driving speed with the gas pedal, and pressed a button when thinking they were driving at target speed (Figure 1B, right pane).

claim: To refresh drivers' memory, the scene was shortly presented moving at the target speed with clear visibility at the beginning of each trial.
source: To refresh drivers' memory, the scene was shortly presented moving at the target speed with clear visibility at the beginning of each trial.

claim: The direction of the effect of contrast on driving speed depended on the type of contrast reduction.

claim: As compared to clear visibility (mean = 85.1 km/hr), the participants drove significantly slower with distance-dependent contrast reduction (mean = 77.3 and 70.9 km/hr for moderate and severe fog, respectively).
source: As compared to clear visibility (mean = 85.1 km/hr), the participants drove significantly slower with distance-dependent contrast reduction (mean = 77.3 and 70.9 km/hr for moderate and severe fog, respectively), but faster with distance-independent reduction (mean = 93.6 and 101.3 km/hr for moderate and severe uniform reduction, respectively; see Figure 3B).

claim: Participants drove faster with distance-independent reduction (mean = 93.6 and 101.3 km/hr for moderate and severe uniform reduction, respectively) compared to clear visibility.
source: As compared to clear visibility (mean = 85.1 km/hr), the participants drove significantly slower with distance-dependent contrast reduction (mean = 77.3 and 70.9 km/hr for moderate and severe fog, respectively), but faster with distance-independent reduction (mean = 93.6 and 101.3 km/hr for moderate and severe uniform reduction, respectively; see Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by measured driving speed data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05) in experiment 2.
source: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05), and the same pattern was observed for all three target speeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The same pattern of driving speed effects was observed for all three target speeds in experiment 2.
source: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05), and the same pattern was observed for all three target speeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data across different speed conditions.

claim: The behavioural results of experiment 2 are consistent with the perceptual results of the first experiment.
source: These behavioural results are consistent with the perceptual results of the first experiment and can be interpreted as follows: distance-dependent contrast reduction induces an overestimation of visual speed that prompts drivers to drive slower, whereas distance-independent contrast reduction evokes an underestimation of visual speed, prompting drivers to drive faster.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results across experiments.

claim: Distance-dependent contrast reduction induces an overestimation of visual speed that prompts drivers to drive slower.
source: These behavioural results are consistent with the perceptual results of the first experiment and can be interpreted as follows: distance-dependent contrast reduction induces an overestimation of visual speed that prompts drivers to drive slower, whereas distance-independent contrast reduction evokes an underestimation of visual speed, prompting drivers to drive faster.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of experimental data from both experiments.

claim: Distance-independent contrast reduction evokes an underestimation of visual speed, prompting drivers to drive faster.
source: These behavioural results are consistent with the perceptual results of the first experiment and can be interpreted as follows: distance-dependent contrast reduction induces an overestimation of visual speed that prompts drivers to drive slower, whereas distance-independent contrast reduction evokes an underestimation of visual speed, prompting drivers to drive faster.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of experimental data from both experiments.

claim: The results of the first two experiments highlight that the distance-dependent contrast reduction experienced in fog evokes perceptual and behavioural effects that are radically opposite to those resulting from the distance-independent contrast reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
source: The results of the first two experiments highlight that the distance-dependent contrast reduction experienced in fog evokes perceptual and behavioural effects that are radically opposite to those resulting from the distance-independent contrast reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
evidence: This claim is based on synthesis of experimental results.

claim: The radical difference between the two types of contrast reduction is striking because in our experiments, the two types of contrast reduction resulted in the same global attenuation of visual contrast.
source: Such a radical difference is striking because in our experiments, the two types of contrast reduction resulted in the same global attenuation of visual contrast.

claim: The global level of contrast is not the only factor affecting perceived speed.
source: This suggests that the global level of contrast is not the only factor affecting perceived speed.

claim: The spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene plays a critical role in perceived speed.
source: The spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene also seems to play a critical role.

claim: In fog, visibility is reduced with distance.
source: In fog, visibility—that is, contrast—is reduced with distance.

claim: When the driver looks straight ahead in fog, the regions of better visibility in the proximity of the vehicle are typically viewed in peripheral vision.

claim: In fog, the distant regions where visibility is impaired fall in the centre of the driver's visual field.

claim: In fog, fog acts as a mask obscuring the central region of the visual field.

claim: Speed perception strongly depends on the visible portion of the visual field.

claim: Speed is overestimated when the central area is occluded.

claim: Speed is underestimated when the peripheral area is masked.

claim: Speed overestimation in fog could result from the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.

claim: An anti-fog is a distance-dependent contrast reduction characterized by an increase of visibility with distance.
source: To test this hypothesis, we created an anti-fog, that is, a distance-dependent contrast reduction characterized by an increase of visibility with distance (see Figure 2D).

claim: The present study reproduced the perceptual bias showing that visual speed is indeed underestimated when contrast is reduced in a distance-independent manner.

claim: The study demonstrates for the first time that an identical global loss of visibility can evoke opposite percepts, depending on the nature of the underlying visual contrast reduction.
source: However, we show that this is only part of the whole picture. In particular, we demonstrate here for the first time that an identical global loss of visibility can evoke opposite percepts, depending on the nature of the underlying visual contrast reduction.

claim: Contrarily to what has been consistently reported in previous studies, a global contrast reduction can also lead to an overestimation of visual speed.

claim: Global contrast reduction can lead to speed overestimation when contrast is not reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene but varies according to their distance from the viewer.
source: This is notably the case when contrast is not reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene but varies according to their distance from the viewer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In fog, contrast reduction is more important for distant than for close objects, generating a distance-dependent visibility gradient between the peripheral and central area of the visual field.
source: For instance, in fog, contrast reduction is more important for distant than for close objects. This generates a distance-dependent visibility gradient between the peripheral and central area of the visual field.

claim: In fog, perceived speed is not determined by the global level of contrast per se, but rather by the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene.
source: Our results show that in this situation, perceived speed is not determined by the global level of contrast per se, but rather by the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene.

claim: Perceived speed is determined by the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.
source: More specifically, perceived speed is determined by the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.

claim: When visibility is better in the peripheral than in the central visual field, as is the case in fog, speed is overestimated.
source: When visibility is better in the peripheral than in the central visual field, as is the case in fog, speed is overestimated.

claim: Inverting the direction of the contrast gradient with anti-fog inverts the perceptual bias such that speed is now underestimated.
source: Inverting the direction of the contrast gradient with anti-fog and thereby obscuring more the peripheral than the central region of the visual field, inverts the perceptual bias such that speed is now underestimated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The results highlight the critical role of the visibility gradient in perceived speed.
source: This highlights the critical role of the visibility gradient in perceived speed, explaining why speed is unexpectedly overestimated in fog despite a global reduction of visibility.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of experimental results.

claim: The results explain why speed is unexpectedly overestimated in fog despite a global reduction of visibility.

claim: The results evidence the direct relationship between perceived and produced speed.

evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of experimental results.

claim: Speed overestimation systematically prompted drivers to drive slower.

claim: Speed underestimation led to faster driving paces.
source: Specifically, speed overestimation systematically prompted drivers to drive slower, whereas speed underestimation led to faster driving paces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the driving experiments.

source: In 'real-life' driving, the roadsides usually include various objects and landmarks as trees, buildings, traffic signs, or pedestrians.

source: Such objects next to the road can have a cognitive influence on driving speed because they constitute potential obstacles that increase the risk of collision (e.g., tree or building if one drives out of the road and cars or pedestrians suddenly crossing the road).

claim: The design prevented cognitive factors from biasing the results.
source: This prevented cognitive factors as those mentioned above to bias our results, but importantly, it also prevented subjects of using these landmarks to estimate moving speed.

source: Indeed, adding landmarks or other 'higher-level' cues would have given the subjects the possibility to use some cognitive strategies to estimate speed.

source: For instance, subjects could have used relative size information of landmarks to infer distances and counted passing them to assess speed.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential cognitive strategies.

claim: At a 'pure' perceptual level, objects next to the road can also contribute to increase peripheral visual flow, thereby altering perceived speed.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina.
source: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina (Shapley and Victor, 1978), the lateral geniculate nucleus (Solomon et al., 2002), and the primary visual cortex (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Polat et al., 1998; Sceniak et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported in the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina (Shapley and Victor, 1978), the lateral geniculate nucleus (Solomon et al., 2002), and the primary visual cortex (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Polat et al., 1998; Sceniak et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported in the primary visual cortex.
source: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina (Shapley and Victor, 1978), the lateral geniculate nucleus (Solomon et al., 2002), and the primary visual cortex (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Polat et al., 1998; Sceniak et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation has been reported in the middle temporal area (MT or V5), an area playing an important role in motion processing.
source: It has also been reported in the middle temporal area (MT or V5), an area playing an important role in motion processing (Pack et al., 2005; Bartels et al., 2008) and speed detection (Maunsell and Van Essen, 1983b), notably via feedforward projections to the medial superior temporal area (Maunsell and van Essen, 1983a; Ungerleider and Desimone, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: MT plays an important role in speed detection.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Linking neurophysiological findings with the effect of contrast on perceived speed in humans is not straightforward.
source: Yet, linking these neurophysiological findings with the effect of contrast on perceived speed in humans is not straightforward.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the complexity of relating neural and perceptual findings.

claim: The observation that MT neurons tuned to high speeds are strongly activated by slow stimuli at low contrast would predict speed overestimation at low contrast.
source: For instance, the observation that MT neurons tuned to high speeds are strongly activated by slow stimuli at low contrast (Pack et al., 2005) would predict speed overestimation at low contrast.

claim: The prediction of speed overestimation from MT neuron activity is the opposite of what has been usually observed with uniform contrast reduction.
source: This is the opposite of what has been usually observed with uniform contrast reduction, including in the current study.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of neurophysiological predictions with experimental results.

claim: The inconsistency between MT neuron activity and perceived speed might be resolved by assuming a bias towards slow speeds when the total MT population activity is low.
source: As stated by Pack et al. (2005), this inconsistency might be resolved by assuming a bias towards slow speeds when the total MT population activity is low.
evidence: This claim is based on a hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Bayesian models of speed perception rely on the assumption that speed 'measurements' are intrinsically noisy.
source: Such a bias towards slow speed is precisely what is proposed by Bayesian models of speed perception (Weiss et al., 2002; Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006). Specifically, these models rely on the assumption that speed 'measurements' are intrinsically noisy, and that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones—resulting in an elevated prior for slow speeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bayesian modeling literature.

claim: Bayesian models assume that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones—resulting in an elevated prior for slow speeds.
source: Such a bias towards slow speed is precisely what is proposed by Bayesian models of speed perception (Weiss et al., 2002; Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006). Specifically, these models rely on the assumption that speed 'measurements' are intrinsically noisy, and that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones—resulting in an elevated prior for slow speeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bayesian modeling literature.

claim: Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast.
source: Whereas Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast (Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006), speed overestimation observed at higher speeds (Thompson et al., 2006) and at low luminance (Hammett et al., 2007) are more difficult to account for.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling literature.

claim: Speed overestimation observed at higher speeds and at low luminance are more difficult for Bayesian models to account for.
source: Whereas Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast (Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006), speed overestimation observed at higher speeds (Thompson et al., 2006) and at low luminance (Hammett et al., 2007) are more difficult to account for.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research literature.

claim: Alternative models have proposed that speed is encoded as 'the ratio of the responses of physiologically plausible temporal filters'.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling literature.
